beats.trigger: ## Grounded Output
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Score them against a 30-claim benchmark and keep the winner.
beats.got: Something about testing checks on AI output. I don't know what a 'claim' is here yet.

beats.trigger: Write one sentence per case: "the missing organisational check was X."
beats.got: Homework before I've seen any reason to care. It smells like a programme.

beats.trigger: **Identify** what a judge can reach: narrow and working beats broad and pretending
beats.got: A learning-objectives list. The last programme had one too. The 'narrow beats broad' line is the only part that sounds like a person wrote it.

beats.trigger: In Module 3 the synthesized answer sat at an uneasy distance: you'd stake your reputation on some of it without knowing which.
beats.got: It leans on a Module 3 I wasn't in. The 'first judge you can defend' idea is fine.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Grounded, and four candidates to measure
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Grounded means traceable to a specific file, number or quote in a source.
beats.got: Grounded means you can trace it to a source. That is not the same as true. It's a modest claim and I'll accept it. 'There is truth out there' is a bit X-Files.

beats.trigger: at 85% each come to about 20% end-to-end: one task in five correct, four in five with a defect, usually where you won't see it.
beats.got: Small error rates multiply over chained steps. I checked the arithmetic and it holds, and it is why long unattended workflows are risky. It was labelled illustrative, which I appreciated.

beats.trigger: Compounding that destroys single-pass reliability builds loop reliability.
beats.got: Check and fix repeatedly and the errors shrink. It assumes the detector catches 90% every round, and the slide says so. That is too tidy, and I'd want to see the detector's real number.

beats.trigger: asking the agent "Are you sure?" returns another answer from the same source, in the same confident voice.
beats.got: Asking the model 'are you sure?' proves nothing. I do that to my own team's slides. 'Later models may fabricate less; the mechanism stays the same' is candid.

beats.trigger: You don't know which detection method catches what matters on *your* output, on *your* strategic question.
beats.got: Don't trust a method on reputation. Run several on your own material and measure. That I can accept, because I can check it myself.

beats.trigger: **3. Citation integrity.** When the briefing cites a source, does the source contain the claim? Catches *citation cargo-cult*.
beats.got: Four checks, each aimed at a different kind of lie: invented, overreached, miscited, contradicted. Clear enough, though 'cargo-cult' is a bit cute.

beats.trigger: Citation integrity caught a quote absent from the linked sanctions order.
beats.got: A real case, with specific findings from specific detectors. The lawyers who cited invented cases is a concrete thing that wasn't possible two years ago. This is the first slide I'd repeat.

beats.trigger: A grounded judge names what it can't catch.
beats.got: The tool you keep comes with a written list of what it misses. That is more honest than most vendor decks I get.

beats.trigger: Grounding is the discipline; fabrication is the failure: invented case law, invented medications, confident numbers nobody can source.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Two runs is a demo, not a measurement.
beats.got: Two runs aren't proof, and it tells me how many runs would be. It is a plain statement of what doesn't work yet, and that is what makes me trust the rest more.

beats.trigger: The winner becomes a judge file you carry into Module 6.
beats.got: Fifty-five minutes, and I'm supposed to end up with a reusable check file. I'll try it.

beats.trigger: Aim for roughly 10% fabrication or misrepresentation: enough wrongness for the detectors to have a job, not nonsense.
beats.got: We deliberately make the AI write a briefing with errors planted in it, to test the checkers. A sensible lab setup, but it's artificial. Real errors may not look like these.

beats.trigger: Why a separate worker? It runs in its own context, so your main session never sees what was fabricated.
beats.got: A separate worker writes the flawed text so I don't see the answers. A blind test, in other words. Fair.

beats.trigger: Thirty is not statistical, but enough to start seeing the pattern.
beats.got: Thirty claims pulled out as the test set. They say openly it isn't statistical. Fine.

beats.trigger: Four helper agents run in parallel on the same claim pool, each with its own detection method and its own output file.
beats.got: Four agents check the same thirty claims at once, each in its own way, and I just wait. That would have been a week of someone's work before.

beats.trigger: It measures precision (of what the detector flagged, how much was ungrounded?), recall (of what the scorer adjudicated as ungrounded, how much did the detector catch?), and coverage
beats.got: Precision and recall are explained in plain terms. I knew roughly what they were, and now I can read a scoreboard. One doubt: the scorer is also an AI, so who checks the scorer?

beats.trigger: The scoreboard IS the explanation. You can point at a row and say *this is why I'm keeping this one*.
beats.got: I can point at a row of numbers and defend my choice instead of just believing the method. That is the 'test it yourself' I wanted. I'd still want a human to check the scorer.

beats.trigger: The "known limit" line names what you measured and decided not to chase.
beats.got: The winning check is saved as a file with its own limits written in. It's small and practical, and a colleague could reuse it.

beats.trigger: Your benchmark had 30 claims. A production judge wants hundreds.
beats.got: What I built is a toy at thirty claims. They said so themselves, and I respect that.

beats.trigger: The pattern (candidates → benchmark → scorer → winner) works for any quality judgment you automate.
beats.got: The method generalises: try several, measure, keep the best. A bit slogan-like, but it is just ordinary engineering practice.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the benchmark and updates the root instructions file with rules for when future sessions run a groundedness check before trusting an output.
beats.got: The agent writes rules into a settings file for next time. Bureaucracy, but automated bureaucracy.

beats.trigger: The agent's report describes what it intended, not what is in the file.
beats.got: Don't trust the agent's report of what it did. Open the file and check. I'd tell that to my team without any AI context.

beats.trigger: If a future session should never trust that shape of output without a check, write the trigger into the root instructions file.
beats.got: Push back on the agent's summary, and be specific about which outputs always need checking.

beats.trigger: Propose, double-check, apply.
beats.got: The agent proposes, a check or a human reviews, then it acts. This is plain change control, and I've seen it before.

beats.trigger: Ask which rung this action has earned.
beats.got: A reading link and a ladder metaphor. I'll read it if I have time.

beats.trigger: Grounded means traceable to a source; accurate is harder.
beats.got: Four short points. 'Grounded is not the same as accurate' is the one worth keeping.

beats.trigger: Ethan Mollick, "Garbage Can and Bitter Lesson."
beats.got: More reading. My inbox is full already.

beats.trigger: Evals scale it to three hundred claims, run the judge on every build, and feed its feedback into generation between rounds.
beats.got: The next step is the same thing at ten times the scale, run automatically. Plausible. I'd wait to see whether the thirty-claim version helps first.

take_homes: Asking the AI 'are you sure?' proves nothing. Check its output against the sources, with something other than the AI's own say-so.
Test the checking methods on your own material and read the scores. Don't pick one on reputation.
Any check I keep should come with a written list of what it misses. Thirty claims is a demo, not proof.

monday.move: Take one AI-written summary that is going to a steering group and check three or four of its numbers against the source files by hand. I'm not building the benchmark yet.
monday.when: Next time such a summary lands, probably within the week
monday.stop_condition: If I find nothing wrong in two or three summaries, I drop it.
monday.blocker: The calendar full of the last programme's steering groups, and not knowing which sources count as the evidence roster.

misconception.why: The real case with named detector findings, plus openly stated limits (two runs is a demo, thirty is not statistical), is not how the last three programmes sold themselves. I still think much of the surrounding hype will blow over, but I no longer think waiting is free: the error arithmetic applies to anyone already using it.

one_line: It was less of a sales pitch than I expected: they tell you what doesn't work yet and give you a way to test it yourself. The prework and the ladder-and-rung stuff are what I'd cut.
